head: o senhor — "you (formal, to a man); sir"
fields: ** Latin seniōrem ("the older one") became senhor: \-ni- → \-nh-. In late and medieval Latin, *senior* became a title for a lord or feudal superior. The article *o* comes from Latin *illum* ("that one"); Portuguese dropped the initial l-.
** English *senior, senate, senile, sir, sire, monsieur*; Spanish *señor*; French *seigneur*; Italian *signore

Latin senex \= old man; senior \= "the older one." Picture the Roman senatus, literally the council of old men: the elders who sat in judgment. In feudal Latin, senior was the lord a vassal served, the elder who protects and commands.

English kept this word too, just worn down: senior → Old French sire → English sire and sir. So "Yes, sir" and "Sim, senhor" are the same word. English also re-borrowed senior straight from Latin for "older" (senior citizen), along with senate and senile.
An elder with white hair; the room quiets and makes space.
o senhor / a senhora vs você
In Brazil, the formal "you" is literally "the gentleman / the lady," so the verb is 3rd person: *O senhor entende?* \= "Does the gentleman understand?"
Use it with older people, strangers in service situations, clients, and anyone you want to show respect to. Pimsleur leans on it because it's always safe.
In some families and regions (common in the interior and the Northeast), children call their parents *o senhor / a senhora*.
Sim, senhor\!* / *Não, senhora\!* add emphasis or deference.
Senhor* also means "Lord" in prayer, and *Nossa Senhora* is "Our Lady" (the Virgin Mary). The everyday exclamation *Nossa\!* ("Wow\!") is short for *Nossa Senhora\!
Rough scale: **o senhor / a senhora** (respectful) → **você** (normal, neutral) → **tu** (intimate; used regionally, see *você*).

head: a senhora — "you (formal, to a woman); ma'am"
fields: ** a \< Latin *illam* ("that one," fem.); *\-a* marks feminine
** a feminine form of *senhor*. Latin had no special feminine of *senior*; Romance built one: Spanish *señora*, Italian *signora*, French *madame* uses a different root (*ma dame* \< *mea domina*).
** "the elder lady" → respectful "you" for a woman
An elder woman with white hair; the room quiets and makes space.

head: americano — "American (masc.)"
fields: ** *América* is named after Amerigo Vespucci; Latin *\-ānus* \= "of, from"
** Vespucci's Latinized name *Americus* was used for the New World on Waldseemüller's 1507 map. The suffix *\-ano* comes directly from Latin *\-ānus*. Feminine: *americana*.
Culture:** In Brazil *americano* usually means from the US. Some Latin Americans point out that everyone in the Americas is *americano*, so you'll also hear *norte-americano* and *estadunidense*.
A name written across a newly drawn coastline; someone standing on that land as one of its people.

head: entende — "(you/he/she) understand(s)"
fields: ** Latin *intendere*, "to stretch toward, aim (the mind) at" → "pay attention to" → "understand." Latin short *i* → *e* (in- → en-), and the 3rd-person ending *\-it* reduced to *\-e* (*intendit* → *entende*).

** English *intend, attend, extend, tend, tension, tendon*; Spanish *entender*; French *entendre* (now "to hear," but the old "understand" sense survives in *bien entendu* and *double entendre*); Italian *intendere

Latin tendere \= to stretch. Romans used it for drawing a bow (arcum tendere) and for pitching a tent by stretching hides over poles. In-tendere \= to stretch toward: pull the string back and aim at a target. Latin applied the same picture to the mind: intendere animum \= "aim the mind at" something, strain your attention toward it. Understanding is the arrow landing.

🧵 SAME ROOT IN ENGLISH — tension (the stretch), tent (stretched cloth), tendon (the cord stretched across a joint), extend (stretch out), attend (stretch toward \= pay attention), pretend (stretch something out in front of you as a screen), tend / tendency (lean in a direction), intense (stretched hard; from intendere itself).

English already had a native word for this sense: understand, from Old English understandan (under \+ standan), recorded well before the Norman Conquest of 1066\. Why "stand under" came to mean "grasp" is debated. One theory is that Old English under could mean "among, between" (like German unter), so the word meant to stand in the middle of a matter, but that's uncertain. When Old French entendre came into Middle English, the "understand" slot was taken, so the borrowing survived in its "aiming" sense: intend \= aim your will at a goal (intent, intention). English then re-spelled it after the Latin in-.

🇫🇷 FRENCH TOOK A THIRD PATH — Old French entendre meant "pay attention to; understand." Over the late Middle Ages and early modern period it narrowed to "hear" (aiming your ears), pushing out the older verb ouïr. French now uses comprendre for "understand." The old sense survives in bien entendu ("of course," lit. "well understood") and in double entendre.

🇧🇷 WHY PORTUGUESE KEPT IT — Portuguese and Spanish (entender) simply kept the late-Latin meaning "aim the mind → grasp it." No native rival word took over that job, so entender stayed the everyday verb. Portuguese doesn't need an "understand." The bow image is the understanding.

compreender \= com \+ prehendere, "seize together": grasp the whole thing (English comprehend, apprehend, prehensile). It's a bit more complete and formal than entender. Perceber \= per \+ capere, "seize thoroughly" (English perceive). In Brazil it mostly means "to notice, realize" (Percebi que… \= I realized that…). Using it as "understand?" (Percebes?) is very typical of Portugal; in Brazil you'll mostly hear Entendeu? Sacar is Brazilian slang for "to get it": Sacou? \= Got it? Its base meaning is "to pull out, draw" (sacar dinheiro \= withdraw cash), and its deeper origin is uncertain.

⚠️ "INTEND" IS NOT ENTENDER — For "intend" Portuguese uses pretender (Pretendo viajar \= I intend to travel). That's a false friend: English "pretend" is fingir in Portuguese. You'll also see tencionar (formal, from tenção "intention," the same tendere root) and ter a intenção de. Related idioms: entender de \= to know about (Ele entende de fotografia), entendido \= an expert, dar a entender \= to hint.
Arm draws the bowstring back to the cheek, eyes locked on the mark. Release. Thud. It lands.

head: entendo — "I understand"
fields: ** *\-o* \= 1st person singular, same as in Latin (*intendo*)
** same as *entende*. The Latin first-person *\-o* survived unchanged; the same thing happened in Spanish and Italian (*entiendo, intendo*).
Arm draws the bowstring back to the cheek, eyes locked on the mark. Release. Thud. It lands.

head: português — "Portuguese (language)"
fields: ** *Portus Cale* (or *Portucale*) was a Roman-era settlement at the mouth of the Douro river, where Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia are today. Its name spread to the county, then the kingdom. *Portus* \= "harbor." The origin of *Cale* is uncertain: possibly pre-Roman, and disputed. Latin *\-ensis* → *\-ês*; the final *\-al* of *Portugal* dropped out of the adjective.
** English *port, passport, opportunity* (from *portus*); the suffix matches English *\-ese* (*Portuguese, Japanese*), Italian *\-ese*, Spanish *\-és*, French *\-ais/-ois
** The ê is closed and stressed: por-tu-GUÊS. Feminine: *portuguesa*. Language names are lowercase.
Latin portus \= harbor, the place where ships pass in from the sea. It's related to porta, "door, gate." Portus Cale was the harbor at the Douro's mouth, a doorway from sea to land.
port, portal, passport ("pass the port"). Traditionally also opportunity (ob portum, "toward the harbor," like a wind that brings you to port), but that explanation is plausible, not certain.
Ships slip through a harbor mouth, a doorway from open sea to land.

head: com licença — "excuse me"
fields: ** English *license, licit, illicit, leisure* (via Old French *loisir* \< *licēre*), prefix *com-/con-* (*combine, connect*); Spanish *con licencia*; Italian *con licenza
It's literally a request for a *license* to act: to get past someone, step into a room or someone's home, interrupt, leave the table, or take something.
It's said *before* the action. *Desculpa / desculpe* ("sorry") is said *after* you bump into someone or make a mistake.
You'll often hear just *Licença\!* in a crowded bus or market.

Common replies: *Pois não* ("of course / go ahead"), *Fique à vontade* ("make yourself comfortable"). A playful Brazilian reply is *Toda\!* ("all of it," meaning you have all the permission you need). That one is informal.
Latin licet \= "it is allowed," a word from law and custom rather than a physical picture. Licentia \= the freedom to act, a granted allowance. No concrete original image is known.

English license took the official-permit sense (driver's license), and licentious took the "too much freedom" sense. For the polite phrase, English says excuse me, from Latin ex \+ causa ("out of the charge/accusation"). English asks to be let off the blame, often after the fact. Portuguese asks for permission before acting.
You pause in a doorway and wait for a nod before stepping through.

head: inglês — "English (language)"
fields: ** the Angles, a Germanic people from Angeln (the Jutland peninsula in modern northern Germany/Denmark); *\-ês* \< Latin *\-ensis

** from the Latin *Angli*. It probably reached Iberian languages through medieval French/Occitan forms like *engleis/anglés*, which explains the *a → e/i* shift. That path is likely but not certain. *Inglaterra* \= "land (*terra*) of the English."
** English *Anglo, Anglican, English*; Spanish *inglés*; French *anglais*; Italian *inglese

** The Brazilian idiom *para inglês ver* ("for the English to see") means "just for show, a facade." It's usually traced to 19th-century Brazilian laws against the slave trade, passed under British pressure and then not enforced. That origin is widely told but not proven.
People of a windswept northern peninsula; their name later carried across the water to an island.

head: eu — "I"
fields: ** English *ego, egotist, egocentric*; Spanish *yo*; Italian *io*; French *je* (also from *eo*)
** Portuguese often drops *eu* because the verb ending already shows the person (*entendo* \= I understand).
English I (Old English ic) and Latin ego come from the same Indo-European word. English wore it down to one letter, Portuguese to eu.
A hand pressed to your own chest.

head: eu sou — "I am"
fields: ** *sou* comes from Latin *sum* "I am" (Old Portuguese *som*; *sou* became standard later). The verb *ser* blends two Latin verbs: *esse* "to be" (which gave *sou, é, são*) and *sedēre* "to sit" (which gave the infinitive *ser*, Old Portuguese *seer*).
** English *essence, essential, absent, present* (*esse*); *sedentary, sediment, preside* (*sedēre*); Spanish *soy*; Italian *sono*; French *suis
** "I am" for identity, origin, profession. *Eu sou americano. Eu sou fotógrafo.
** *ser* is for what something *is* (identity, origin). *estar* is for state and location (see *onde está?* in Lesson 4).
ser is built from two Latin verbs: esse "to be" (sou, é, são) and sedēre "to sit" (the infinitive ser, Old Portuguese seer). A memory aid, not etymology: what you are is where you're seated.
English has the same ancient roots but keeps them as separate verbs: is shares its source with Latin est, and sit is the Germanic cousin of sedēre. Portuguese merged them into one verb.
A hand pressed to your chest as you sit firmly planted — not just where you happen to stand, but who you are.

head: é — "is; you are (formal)"
fields: ** single verb form (3rd person singular of *ser*)
** English *is* (same Indo-European root), *essence*; Spanish *es*; French *est*; Italian *è
A stone set in the earth, simply there, by its nature.

head: por favor — "please"
fields: ** *por* \< Latin *pro* "for, on behalf of" (blended with *per* "through"); *favor* \< Latin *favor* "goodwill, support," from *favēre* "to be well-disposed"
** both words came straight from Latin with little change.
** English *favor, favorite, favorable, pro-*; Spanish *por favor*; Italian *per favore
** Formal signs and polite requests also use *por gentileza* (see *gentil*). *Faz favor* is more typical of Portugal.

Latin favēre \= to be well-disposed toward someone, to back them. At Roman rites the call favete linguis ("favor with your tongues") meant "keep holy silence," so no ill-omened word would spoil the ceremony. Favor \= goodwill shown.

English kept favor almost unchanged, but its polite word is please, short for "if you please," from Latin placēre (the same root as prazer). English says "if it pleases you"; Portuguese says "as a favor."
An open hand, offered with warmth, asking a kindness in return.

head: de — "of, from"
fields: ** English prefix *de-* (*descend, depart, detach*); Spanish/French *de*; Italian *di
** origin (*sou de Nova York*), possession (*o livro de Zach*), material (*de madeira*)
** It merges with articles: de \+ o \= **do**, de \+ a \= **da**, de \+ os \= **dos**, de \+ as \= **das**.
Something coming away from its source.

head: um pouco — "a little"
fields: ** *unum* → *um* (the n became nasalization); *paucum* → *pouco* (au → ou, a regular change).
** English *one, unit, unique* (*unus*); *paucity* (*paucus*), and English *few* shares the same ancient root; music term *poco a poco*; Spanish *un poco*; Italian *un poco*; French *un peu
** *Falo um pouco de português* \= "I speak a little Portuguese." Brazilians love the diminutive *um pouquinho* ("a tiny bit").
English few is the Germanic relative of Latin paucus (same Indo-European root). Paucity is the learned borrowing.
A pinch held between two fingers — just that much.

head: bom dia — "good morning"
fields: ** *bonum* → *bom* (final \-n became a nasal vowel); feminine *boa* \< *bona* (intervocalic n dropped). Latin *diēs* → Vulgar Latin *dia*.

** English *bonus, bona fide, bounty*; *diary, dial, diurnal, meridian*, and *journal* (via *diurnalis*); Spanish *buenos días*; French *bonjour* and Italian *buongiorno* (both use *diurnum* for "day")
** *dia* is masculine despite the \-a (*o dia*), so it's ***bom** dia*, not *boa dia*.
Bom dia:** from waking up until about noon or lunch.
Boa tarde:** from noon until dusk (roughly 6 pm).
Boa noite:** after dark, both as "good evening" when arriving and "good night" when leaving.
Brazilians greet a room, a shop, or an elevator with these. Walking into a store without a *bom dia* can seem a bit cold.

Latin diēs comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to shine," the bright sky. The same root gives Latin deus (god) and divine, Iuppiter (from "sky-father"), and Greek Zeus. A day is "the bright sky."

English day looks like dia but is NOT related: it's Germanic, from a different root. English uses diēs only in learned words: diary, diurnal, meridian ("midday"), and via French journal and journey (originally a day's travel).
Morning light floods the sky; you greet someone under the brightness.

head: até logo — "see you later; goodbye"
fields: ** *até* \= "until, up to; even"; *logo* \< Latin *locō* "in the place"

** *logo*: Latin *locō* ("on the spot") → "immediately" → "soon." *até*: **disputed.** It's often traced to Arabic *ḥattā* "until" (also proposed for Spanish *hasta*), a legacy of centuries of Arabic presence in Iberia. Latin sources have also been proposed.
** *locō*: English *local, location, locomotive, locus*; Spanish *hasta luego* (*luego* \= *logo*)
Até logo* is a friendly, neutral goodbye and doesn't have to mean the same day.
Family: *até amanhã* (until tomorrow), *até mais* (until later), *até já* (see you in a moment, more common in Portugal).
The most common casual Brazilian goodbye is **tchau**, from Italian *ciao*, which comes from Venetian *s-ciao* "(I am your) slave," originally a deferential greeting, from Latin *sclavus*.
Logo* also means "therefore": *Penso, logo existo* \= "I think, therefore I am."
logo is Latin locō, "in the place": right on the spot. "On the spot" → "immediately" → "soon." English makes the same move when it says "I'll do it on the spot."
⚠️ NOTE — até has no confirmed Latin image. Arabic ḥattā "until" is the leading theory, but it's disputed.
You part on a path and point back to the same spot, to meet there again soon.

head: obrigado — "thank you (said by a man)"
fields: ** Latin *obligātus*, past participle of *obligāre* "to bind (to someone)." Two regular sound changes: b \+ l → **br** (*obligare* → *obrigar*), and intervocalic \-t- → \-d- (*\-atum* → *\-ado*).
** English *oblige, obligation, "much obliged," ligament, ligature, liable, ally, rely* (from Latin *religare* via Old French); Spanish *obligado* (but Spanish uses it for "forced," not "thanks")

Saying *obrigado* literally means "I'm in your debt," like old English "much obliged" or "I'm beholden to you." Spanish and Italian thank by giving grace (*gracias, grazie*); Portuguese thanks by declaring a debt.

It describes **the speaker**, so it agrees with the speaker's gender: men say *obrigado*, women say *obrigada*, regardless of who they're thanking. In casual speech you'll sometimes hear the gender ignored.
Replies: *De nada* ("of nothing"), *Por nada*, *Não há de quê* ("there's nothing to thank for"), and the very Brazilian *Imagina\!* ("imagine \[that you'd owe me\]," like "don't mention it").

Latin ligāre \= to tie, bind (a ligament ties bone to bone). Ob-ligāre \= to tie toward: a rope runs from you to the person who helped you. Roman law defined an obligatio as a legal bond (iuris vinculum), a debt you're tied to.

English kept obliged ("much obliged") but thanks with thank, a Germanic word related to think. To thank is, at root, to "think of" someone's kindness. English says "I'll remember you"; Portuguese says "I'm tied to you."

The same rope is in ligar \= to connect, switch on, or phone (Liga pra mim \= call me). Ligado \= switched on, tuned in. Não ligo \= I don't care (I'm not connected to it). Also obrigação \= obligation and obrigatório \= mandatory.
A cord loops around your wrist and ties you to the person who just helped you.

head: obrigada — "thank you (said by a woman)"
fields: ** same as *obrigado*; *\-a* marks a feminine speaker
A cord loops around your wrist and ties you to the person who just helped you.

head: muito — "very; a lot"
fields: ** It's pronounced with a nasal "ũi" (roughly "MŨY-too") even though there's no tilde. This is a well-known quirk.
Latin multus \= many, much: a multitude, a crowded street.

For everyday speech English uses the Germanic much (Old English micel, "great, big") and keeps multi- for learned words (multiply, multimedia). Portuguese muito and Spanish mucho are just multum worn down.
A packed street, people pressed shoulder to shoulder.

head: muito bem — "very well"
fields: ** Spanish *muy bien*; Italian *molto bene*; French *très bien
** It's also praise, "Well done\!", the way a teacher would say it. *Estou muito bem* \= "I'm very well."
A teacher's hands open wide, a deep nod, again and again.

head: bem — "well; fine"
fields: ** Latin *bene* → *bem* (final \-e lost, n became a nasal vowel). Portuguese keeps a plain e where Spanish breaks it into *ie* (*bien*).
** English *benefit, benevolent, benediction, benign*; Spanish *bien*; French *bien*; Italian *bene
** As a noun: *meu bem* \= "my dear, darling" (very common endearment); *bens* \= goods, assets.
Latin bene \= well, rightly (its adjective is bonus, "good"). There's no clear physical image, and its origin beyond Old Latin is uncertain.
Everyday English well is Germanic. Bene survives only in compounds: benefit ("done well"), benediction ("well-speaking" \= blessing), benevolent ("well-wishing").
The body at ease, everything running smoothly, nothing catching.

head: tudo bem — "all good; how's it going?"
fields: ** English *total, totality, tutti* (music); Spanish *todo bien*; Italian *tutto bene*; French *tout va bien
Tudo bem?* is the default Brazilian greeting, and *Tudo bem* is the default answer. *Tudo bem? — Tudo bem, e você?* Like "How's it going? — Good, you?", it's a ritual, not a real health check.
Variants: *Tudo bom? — Tudo ótimo\!*, *Tudo certo?*, *E aí, tudo bem?* ("Hey, all good?"), the casual *Beleza?* ("Beauty?" \= "Cool?").
It also means "It's OK / no problem" after an apology: *Desculpa\! — Tudo bem.
It often comes with a thumbs up, which Brazilians call *joia* ("jewel").
** *tudo* (everything, unchanging) vs *todo/toda* ("all, the whole," agrees with its noun).
Latin tōtus \= whole, entire, undivided. English total; in music, tutti \= "everyone plays."
The whole scene is at ease — nothing out of place.

head: como — "how"
fields: ** English *mode, model, modify, modest* (*modus*); Spanish *cómo*; Italian *come*; French *comment* (*quomodo* \+ *\-ment*)
** *como* also means "as, like" (*como eu* \= like me), and *como* \= "I eat" (from *comer*, a different Latin word, *comedere*). *Como como?* \= "How do I eat?"
Latin modus first meant a measure (a measured amount, a rhythm, a limit), then a "way of doing." Quō modō \= "by what measure?" → "how?"
English asks with Germanic how, but the measure root lives on in mode, model ("a small measure"), modest (keeping to measure), moderate, modify.
You tilt your head, measuring the way a thing is being done.

head: vai — "goes; (you/he/she) go(es)"
fields: ** vai (3rd person singular present of *ir* "to go")

** *ir* is built from three Latin verbs: *vādere* "to go, walk" gives *vou, vai, vamos, vão*; *īre* "to go" gives the infinitive *ir*; and *esse* "to be" gives the past *fui* (so *fui* \= both "I went" and "I was").
** English *invade, evade, pervasive* (*vādere*); *exit, transit, itinerary* (*īre*); Spanish *va*; French *va*; Italian *va
Latin vādere \= to go, stride forward, often with purpose. It's probably related to vadum, "a ford" (a shallow crossing). English wade is its Germanic cousin.

English uses Germanic go. Vādere shows up in invade (stride in), evade (stride out of reach), pervasive (going through everything). English mixes verbs too: went was borrowed from wend. That's like Portuguese ir, which mixes vou/vai (vādere), ir (īre) and fui (esse).
A body wading forward through a shallow crossing, stride after stride.

head: como vai? — "how are you?"
fields: ** French *Comment ça va?*; Spanish *¿Cómo te va?*; Italian *Come va?*; German *Wie geht's?*; old English *How goes it?
** It's a bit more polite or classic than *Tudo bem?*. Typical answer: *Vou bem, obrigado, e você?* ("I go well, thanks, and you?") or just *Bem, obrigado.
Someone walks toward you; you watch the pace and the set of their shoulders.

head: como vai o senhor? — "how are you? (formal, to a man)"
fields: ** the respectful version of *como vai?*. The verb stays 3rd person because you're grammatically talking *about* "the gentleman."
Culture:** Use it with an older man, a hotel manager, a client.
The white-haired elder walks in; you watch how his steps are going, and the room makes space.

head: como vai a senhora? — "how are you? (formal, to a woman)"
fields: ** a respectful greeting to a woman, especially an older one
The elder woman walks in; you watch how her steps are going, and the room makes space.

head: de onde — "from where"
fields: ** Latin *unde* meant "*from* where," but in Portuguese *onde* drifted to plain "where." So Portuguese added *de* again: *de onde* is historically "from from-where." Spanish *donde* is itself *de \+ unde* fused, which makes *¿de dónde?* a double-double.
** *De onde você é?* \= "Where are you from?" Also *aonde* \= "to where" (a \+ onde).
Latin unde \= "from which place, whence": looking back down the road someone came by.
English has its own whence (Germanic), but it's archaic, so English says "from where." Portuguese onde lost its "from" meaning, so it needed de again.
You turn and look back down the road, to the place someone came from.

head: boa tarde — "good afternoon"
fields: ** *bona* → *boa* (intervocalic n dropped). The adverb *tardē* ("late") became a noun meaning "the late part of the day."
** English *tardy, retard* (to delay), *ritardando*; Spanish *buenas tardes*; French *tard* ("late"); Italian *tardi
** *tarde* is feminine, so it's *boa*. As an adverb it still means "late": *É tarde* \= "It's late." Use it from noon to dusk.
Latin tardus \= slow, sluggish, late. As a memory aid (not etymology), the afternoon is the slow, late stretch of the day as the sun drags toward evening.
tardy (late to class); retard originally meant "to slow down"; ritardando in music \= slowing.
The sun hangs lower, the air slows; you greet someone in the late light.

head: brasileiro — "Brazilian (masc.)"
fields: ** Brasil \+ \-eiro (one who deals with / belongs to)
** *Brasil* (see below); *\-eiro* \< Latin *\-ārius* "connected with, one who does"

** Latin *\-ārium* → *\-eiro* (the i moved forward: *\-ariu* → *\-airo* → *\-eiro*). *\-eiro* normally marks professions (*padeiro* baker, *carpinteiro* carpenter). It's often noted that *brasileiro* originally meant someone who traded brazilwood, which explains why the word isn't the expected *brasiliense* or *brasiliano*.
A merchant with arms full of red dyewood — the one who works that timber.

head: brasileira — "Brazilian (fem.)"
fields: ** "Brazilian woman" or a feminine noun (*a música brasileira*)
A woman with arms full of red dyewood — the one who works that timber.

head: você — "you (informal)"
fields: ** contraction of *Vossa Mercê* ("Your Grace / Your Mercy")

** an honorific worn down by centuries of use: *vossa mercê* → *vossemecê* → *vosmecê* → *você* → colloquial *ocê* → *cê*. Because it was originally "Your Grace," it takes a 3rd-person verb: *você é*.
** English *mercy, mercenary, merchant* share the *merc-* "pay, trade" root; Spanish *usted* comes from *vuestra merced*, the exact same idea.
In most of Brazil, *você* is the normal, neutral "you" for friends, peers, and strangers your age.
Tu* is common in some regions (Rio Grande do Sul, parts of the Northeast, Pará, and casually in Rio), often with a 3rd-person verb (*tu vai*), which is grammatically "wrong" but normal speech.
In Portugal, *você* can sound distant or even slightly rude, and *tu* is the informal norm. This is a generalization; usage varies.

Latin mercēs \= pay, wages, related to merx "merchandise" (market, merchant, commerce). Church Latin used it for the reward God grants, which became "grace, mercy." Vossa Mercê \= "Your Grace / Your Favor."

English mercy kept the "compassion" sense, and French merci became "thank you." English "Your Grace" is the exact equivalent of vossa mercê, but English kept it for dukes and archbishops and never wore it down into an everyday "you."
An old formal bow, worn down by years into a casual nod, still aimed at the other person, not at yourself.

head: você é — "you are (informal)"
fields: That same nod, then a quiet naming of who they are, as if speaking of someone a step apart from you.

head: como vai você? — "how are you? (informal)"
fields: ** a friendly *como vai?*. Answer: *Vou bem, e você?
You watch the other person's stride, still from a slight formal distance.

head: dos — "of the; from the"
fields: ** *de* \+ *os* fused into one word. Portuguese merges prepositions with articles all the time (*do, da, no, na, pelo*).
** Many countries take an article: *o Brasil* → *do Brasil*; *os Estados Unidos* → *dos Estados Unidos*. But *Portugal* has none: *de Portugal*.
Several things coming away from a group, down from that source.

head: Estados Unidos — "United States"
fields: ** Latin *status* → *estado* (e- added before s \+ consonant, t → d). *ūnītos* → *unidos* (t → d).
** English *state, status, estate, station, statue; united, union, unit*; Spanish *Estados Unidos*; French *États-Unis* (*estat* lost its s, marked by the é)
** The plural article sticks: *os Estados Unidos são...
Latin stāre \= to stand; status \= how something stands, its standing. Ūnus \= one, so unidos \= "made one."
Here English kept both roots directly: state, status, estate, statue (a standing figure); unite, union, unit. No split.
Separate posts standing in a row, then bound into a single bundle.

head: Brasil — "Brazil"
fields: ** bras(a) (ember, glowing coal) \+ \-il (suffix; the exact formation is uncertain)
** probably from *brasa* "ember," for the glowing red dye

** named after **pau-brasil** (brazilwood), a red dyewood that was the colony's first major export. *Brasil* was already a name for red dyewoods in medieval European trade, before 1500\. Deriving it from *brasa* "ember" is the most accepted explanation, but not certain; links to the legendary Atlantic island "Hy-Brasil" have also been proposed. When Pedro Álvares Cabral arrived in 1500, the land was first called *Ilha de Vera Cruz*, then *Terra de Santa Cruz*, before *Brasil* took over.
** Portuguese spells it with **s**; English with **z**.
A stick of wood glowing like a coal, red dye seeping from it.

head: boa noite — "good evening; good night"
fields: ** *noctem* → *noite* (-ct- → \-it-, the signature Portuguese change; Spanish has *noche*).
** English *night* (Germanic relative), *nocturnal, nocturne, equinox*; French *nuit*; Italian *notte
** Unlike English, one phrase covers both "good evening" (arriving at 8 pm dinner) and "good night" (leaving or going to bed). Switch from *boa tarde* at dusk.
A true cognate: Latin noctem and English night come from the same Indo-European word. Also nocturnal and equinox ("equal night").
Darkness settles; a quiet greeting as the sky goes black.

head: de Nova York — "from New York"
fields: ** *nova* kept its Latin form. Portuguese doesn't break the o into *ue* the way Spanish does (*Nueva York*). *York* goes back to Old English *Eoforwīc*, from Latin *Eboracum*, from a Celtic name probably meaning "place of yews." New York was named in 1664 for the Duke of York (later James II).
** English *novel, novice, innovate, renovate, nova*; Spanish *Nueva York
** Brazilian spelling is *Nova York*; *Nova Iorque* is the Portugal/standard spelling. *de novo* \= "again."
Latin novus and English new are true cognates. A nova is a "new" star.
Stepping away from a vast harbor city of towers.

head: onde está? — "where is?"
fields: ** English *stand* (Germanic relative), *stable, static, station, stay* (via Old French *ester*); Spanish *está*; Italian *sta
** "where does it stand?" \= where is it (right now)?
** *estar* \= temporary state or location; *ser* \= identity. In speech, *está* is often shortened to **tá**: *Onde tá?*, *Tá bom* ("OK"). *Onde está o hotel?
Latin stāre \= to stand: something upright in its spot right now.
English stand is the Germanic cousin of stāre. English uses "is" for location; Portuguese asks "where does it stand?" Ser \= be (by essence); estar \= stand (for now).
You scan the room for something upright in its spot, right now.

head: onde fica? — "where is (it located)?"
fields: ** *ficar* \< Vulgar Latin \**figicāre*, from Latin *fīgere* "to fix, fasten"
** \**figicāre* (reconstructed) → *ficar*: "to be fixed" → "to remain, stay" → "to be located." Spanish has *fincar* ("to plant, fix") and Italian *ficcare* ("to thrust in").
** English *fix, fixture, affix, prefix, suffix, crucifix
** "where is it fixed?", which is why it's used for buildings, cities, and things that don't move
** *ficar* is one of Brazil's busiest verbs:
Fica à vontade* \= "make yourself at home"
slang *ficar com alguém* \= to hook up or make out casually, without dating
Latin fīgere \= to fix, fasten, drive in: hammering a nail or stake so something can't move. A crucifix is something fixed to a cross. Ficar comes from a reconstructed Late Latin form, \*figicāre.
English got fix from the Latin participle fixus, but for these senses it uses stay (from Old French ester \< stāre, "to stand") or "be located."
You look for the place a stake was driven — fixed, unmoving.

head: o hotel — "the hotel"
fields: ** Late Latin *hospitāle* → Old French *hostel* → French *hôtel* (the circumflex marks the lost s) → borrowed into Portuguese as *hotel*. The **h is silent** and the stress is on the end: o-TÉL. Plural: *hotéis*.
** a family of doublets from one Latin word: English *hospital, hostel, hotel, host, hospitality, hospice*; Portuguese *hospital, hóspede* (guest), *hospedar* (to host)

Latin hospes meant both host AND guest, the two sides of the sacred bond between a traveler and the household that took him in. A hospitāle was a guest house. Its deeper origin is often reconstructed as "lord of strangers" (\*ghosti-pot-), which is widely cited but uncertain.

English took this root several times, and each borrowing got a different job: hospital (first a shelter for travelers and the needy), hostel and host (via Old French), hotel (later, from modern French hôtel), hospitality, hospice.
A traveler crossing a threshold, received as both guest and host in the same house.

head: o restaurante — "the restaurant"
fields: ** o (the) \+ re- (again, back) \+ staur- (make firm, restore) \+ \-ante (present participle "-ing")
** Latin *restaurāre* \= "to restore, rebuild"; the root of *\-staurāre* is uncertain; *\-ante* \= "-ing"
** French *restaurant*, "restoring," was first a restorative broth. In the 1760s–70s it came to mean the Paris eating-houses that served such food, and the word spread worldwide, Portuguese included.
** The initial **r sounds like English h**: "hes-tau-RAN-chee" (in much of Brazil, *\-te* sounds like "chee").
Latin restaurāre \= to rebuild, renew, repair something worn down, like a temple or a wall. In 18th-century Paris a restaurant was a restorative broth, then the shop that sold it.
English uses the root both ways, restore and restaurant. No split, just a French detour. Portuguese restaurar still means to restore (restaurar um quadro \= restore a painting).
A worn body sitting down to a meal and feeling itself rebuilt.

head: minha — "my (fem.)"
fields: ** Latin *mea* → Old Portuguese *mia / mĩa* → *minha*. Nasalization spread from the initial m and later became written *nh*. Masculine *meu* \< Latin *meum*.
** English *my, mine, me* (Germanic relatives); Spanish *mía / mi*; Italian *mia*; French *ma
** "my," agreeing with the thing owned: *minha mala* (fem.), *meu hotel* (masc.)
Latin mea/meum and English me/my/mine share the same Indo-European root.
Your hand closes over something that is yours.

head: mala — "suitcase"
fields: ** Old French *male* "bag, pouch" (modern French *malle* "trunk"), from Frankish \**malha*, a Germanic word.
** English **mail** comes from the same Old French *male*: the mailbag came first, then the letters inside. Spanish *maleta*.
** *porta-malas* \= car trunk ("carry-bags"). Brazilian slang: *ele é um mala* \= "he's a pain, a bore" (dead weight you have to carry).
Frankish \*malha, a traveler's bag or pouch. It's Germanic, not Latin.
English mail is the same word: first the mailbag, then the letters inside.
A traveler's bag in the hand, a pouch ready for the road.

head: aqui — "here"
fields: ** Vulgar Latin \**accu hīc* ("look, here\!") → *aqui*. The emphatic "look" piece fused on.
** Three-way "here/there": **aqui** (here, near me) → **aí** (there, near you) → **ali / lá** (over there). *E aí?* \= "What's up?" (lit. "and there?").
Vulgar Latin \*accu hīc ≈ "look\! here\!": a pointing gesture at the ground, built into the word.
There's no everyday English cognate, but the same Latin "this/here" family appears in ad hoc ("for this").
A finger jabs at the ground at your feet: right here.

head: fica lá — "it's (located) there"
fields: ** *lá* is everywhere in casual speech. *Sei lá* (lit. "I know there") \= "who knows / no idea," often with a shrug.
lá \< Latin illāc, "that way, over there."
You point into the distance, to a spot already fixed in place, over there.

head: muito prazer — "nice to meet you"
fields: ** muito (much) \+ praz- (please) \+ \-er (infinitive, used as a noun)
** *prazer* \< Latin *placēre* "to please"; the infinitive works as a noun ("pleasure")
** *placēre* → *prazer*. Two regular changes: pl → pr (consonant \+ l → r) and intervocalic c → z (like *facere* → *fazer*, *dicere* → *dizer*).

** English *please, pleasure, placid, complacent, placebo* ("I will please"); Spanish *mucho gusto* (different word) / *placer*; French *plaisir*; Italian *piacere* (also how Italians say "nice to meet you")
Said when you're introduced. Replies: *O prazer é meu* ("the pleasure is mine") or *Igualmente* ("likewise").

It often comes with a handshake. In social settings Brazilians, especially women, greet with cheek kisses; the number varies by region and person (often one in São Paulo, two in Rio), so follow the other person's lead.
Latin placēre \= to please, be agreeable. It's often linked to placāre (to calm, soothe), but the deeper image behind the root is uncertain.

English kept please and pleasure, but for introductions it says "nice to meet you." Nice comes from Latin nescius ("not knowing, ignorant") and meant "foolish" in Middle English before softening to "pleasant." Portuguese just says "much pleasure."
A warm, easy smile spreading as you meet someone, like a pleasant taste.

head: gentil — "kind"
fields: ** Latin *gēns, gentis* \= "clan, family" (root *gen-* "birth, kin"); *\-ilis* \= adjective suffix
** Latin *gentīlis* "of the same clan" → "well-born, noble" (Old French *gentil*) → "courteous, kind."
** English *gentle, gentleman, genteel, gentile, genus, gene, generate, genre, genial*; Spanish *gentil*; French *gentil* ("nice"); Italian *gentile* ("kind")
Portuguese *gentil* means kind, polite, considerate. It's a strong compliment: *Você é muito gentil* \= "That's very kind of you."

Gentileza gera gentileza* ("kindness generates kindness") is a famous Rio motto from the street preacher José Datrino, known as **Profeta Gentileza**. His murals on a Rio viaduct are now a protected landmark.

Latin gēns \= clan, a Roman extended family sharing a name (the gens Julia was Julius Caesar's clan). Gentīlis \= "belonging to a clan," a free, well-born Roman rather than an outsider. Courtly Old French gentil \= noble → noble manners → kind.

English borrowed the word several times, and each copy froze a different stage: gentile (Church Latin gentiles, "the nations," meaning non-Jews), gentle (noble → mild), genteel (re-borrowed from French, "refined"), and jaunty (also from French gentil). Portuguese kept just one meaning: kind.
A courteous hand, a soft voice — the easy manners of someone raised in a close clan.

head: eu não sei — "I don't know"
fields: eu \< Latin ego; não \< Latin nōn "not"; sei is the irregular 1st-person present of saber, "to know"

Latin nōn became Portuguese não (the tilde marks a nasal vowel). sei belongs to saber, from Latin sapere "to taste, to have flavor." That physical sense developed a mental one: to have discernment, to be wise, to know. The 1st-person present is irregular: eu sei, not \*sabo (compare Spanish sé, French sais, Italian so).
English savor, sapient, sage, insipid, Homo sapiens; Spanish saber / no sé; French savoir / je ne sais pas; Italian sapere / non so

Latin sapere \= to taste, to have flavor. Taste is the first test of what is in front of you: bitter or sweet, sound or spoiled. From that bodily judgment came "to have discernment," then "to know, to be wise." Homo sapiens is literally "the tasting / wise human." Latin nōn is simply "not," the same particle that English keeps in non-.
English know is Germanic (related to can, cunning, and ken). The Latin root survived in English as savor (taste), sapient and sage (wise), insipid ("without taste"), and sapiens.

saber, sei, sabe, sabemos, sabia; não sei; quem sabe ("who knows"); sabor (taste, flavor); sábio (wise); sabedoria (wisdom); saboroso (tasty). Casual sei lá ("dunno / who knows," literally "I know there") often comes with a shrug.
You taste and find nothing — a slow shake of the head, empty hands.

head: você sabe — "you know"
fields: sabe is the 3rd-person present of saber. você takes 3rd-person verbs because it comes from Vossa Mercê, "Your Grace."
the same Latin sapere "to taste" → "to know," as in eu não sei. The 3rd-person sabe is the regular present of saber.
same family as eu não sei: savor, sapient, sapiens; Spanish sabe; French sait; Italian sa
The same tasting root as sei: the flavor is there this time. You have sampled it, and you know.
Same split as eu não sei: English know is Germanic; savor / sapient / sapiens keep the Latin root.
sabe, você sabe?, sabe? (a spoken filler, like English "you know?"), sabido, saber de cor (to know by heart).
The flavor lands on the tongue; your eyes light up — you have it.

head: o real — "the Brazilian real (currency)"
fields: o \< Latin illum "that one"; real \< Latin rēgālis "royal," from rēx, rēgis "king"

Portuguese and Brazilian money have been called real ("the royal one") for centuries. The old plural was réis (as in mil-réis). After a string of 20th-century currencies (cruzeiro, cruzado, cruzeiro real), the modern real was introduced on July 1, 1994, under the Plano Real, the stabilization plan that ended Brazil's hyperinflation. One real \= 100 centavos. The modern plural is reais, not réis. Symbol: R\$.

English royal, regal, realm, rex; Spanish real (the old silver coin, and "royal"). Portuguese also has a look-alike real meaning "actual, real," from a different Latin word, realis ("of a thing," from rēs). The currency is the royal word, not the "actual" one. English real ("actual") is that second root.
In much of Brazil the initial r of real sounds like English h: "hey-AL."
A king's title stamped on a coin: money that is "royal."
regal and royal are the same Latin word. English real ("actual") is a look-alike from realis, not rēgālis.
reais (plural); centavo; Plano Real. The homonym real / realmente ("actual / really") is from realis, not from "royal."

The Plano Real (1994), associated with finance minister (later president) Fernando Henrique Cardoso, replaced the cruzeiro real and anchored prices to a new unit. Later note series feature Brazilian animals; the 20-reais note's golden lion tamarin is one example.
A Brazilian one-real note, the word REAL under the republic's laurel-crowned head.

head: reais — "reais (Brazilian currency, plural)"
fields: the modern plural of o real
same Latin rēgālis "royal." The historical plural of the old real was réis, which was also the name of the currency for a long time (the réis / mil-réis). After 1994 the official plural is reais.
same as o real: royal, regal; the old Portuguese réis (a different plural of the same word)
"royal ones" → the modern plural of the currency
Pronounced roughly "hey-ICE" in much of Brazil (initial r like English h).
The same royal stamp, now on more than one coin or note.
same as o real: regal, royal. English has no everyday plural of this currency name in common use; Portuguese does: reais.
A Brazilian twenty-reais note, a golden lion tamarin on a branch, the words VINTE REAIS along the edge.

head: você tem — "you have"
fields: tem is the 3rd-person present of ter, "to have"; você again takes the 3rd person.

Latin tenēre "to hold, keep" became Portuguese ter. In classical Latin, habēre was the main verb for "to have," and tenēre was "to hold." Spanish still uses both (tener for possession, haber as auxiliary and existential). Older Portuguese also used haver for possession; over time ter took over "to have / to possess," and haver shrank mainly to the existential há ("there is") and some auxiliary uses (havia, haver de).
English tenacious, tenure, tenant, retain, contain, maintain, tenet, lieutenant; Spanish tener; French tenir ("to hold"); Italian tenere
Latin tenēre \= to hold, to keep in the hand and not let go. To have something is, at root, to hold it.

English have is Germanic (related to heft). The Latin root survived in tenacious (holding tight), tenure (the holding of an office or land), tenant (one who holds land), retain, contain, maintain, and tenet (a belief you hold).
ter, tenho, tem, temos, têm, tinha, tido; manter (to keep, maintain); conteúdo; ter que / ter de ("to have to"). Há (from haver) is "there is," not "he has."
Your hands close around something and keep it.

head: eu tenho — "I have"
fields: the same Latin tenēre "to hold." The 1st-person present tenho shows the palatal \-nh- that developed in this verb (Latin tenēō).
Spanish tengo; French tiens; Italian tengo; English tenacious, tenure, tenant
The same holding image as você tem, now from your own side: your hands, your grip.
Same split as você tem: English have is Germanic; tenacious, tenure, tenant keep the Latin root.
Your own hands close around something and keep it.

head: um — "one; a (masc.)"
fields: Latin ūnus, ūnum "one." Portuguese um is both the number "one" and the indefinite article "a / an," just as English a / an comes from one (an was originally the same word as one). The \-n of ūnum nasalized the vowel and then dropped as a consonant, leaving um. Feminine uma \< Latin ūnam.

English one, an, unit, unique, union, unanimous, universe, onion (from ūniō, "oneness," then a single onion); Spanish un / una; French un / une; Italian un / una. (French une is a look-alike; the Portuguese feminine is uma.)
Latin ūnus \= one, a single thing, not two.

one is the Germanic cousin of ūnus. English later re-borrowed the Latin family: unit, unique, union, unanimous, universe. The indefinite article a / an is historically the same word as one, worn down.
um, uma, uns, umas; único; união; unir; um pouco (already in Lesson 1).
One finger held up; a single thing resting in the palm.

head: uma — "one; a (fem.)"
fields: "one" and also "a / an," agreeing with a feminine noun (uma mala, uma senhora)
Latin ūnam, the feminine of ūnus, became uma. Masculine um \< ūnum.
Spanish una; French une; Italian una; English one, an, unit, unique
The same single thing as um, now agreeing with a feminine noun.
same as um: one, a / an, unit, unique.
One finger held up; a single thing resting in the palm.

head: dólar — "dollar"
fields: German Thaler, shortened from Joachimsthaler, a silver coin first minted in 1518 in Joachimsthal (today Jáchymov, in the Czech Republic). German Thal / Tal means "valley," so a Joachimsthaler is a coin from Joachim's Valley. The coin and the name spread across Europe (Dutch daalder, Swedish daler, Spanish dólar, and the widely used Spanish dollar or piece of eight). English dollar comes from the same Thaler, famously by way of that Spanish dollar. Portuguese dólar is a later borrowing for the US (and other) dollar.
English dollar; German Thaler; Dutch daalder; Swedish daler
a coin named for Joachim's Valley, shortened and borrowed worldwide
Silver coins streaming out of a mountain valley — the valley of Joachim — and traveling the world under a shortened name.
dollar is the same word. No split: Portuguese borrowed the international name.
dólar, dólares; câmbio (exchange). In Brazil o dólar usually means the US dollar unless another is specified.
The US dollar shows up in Brazilian travel, electronics, and export talk; prices are often compared to o dólar. The Thaler also left a wider mark on coinage (for example the Maria Theresa thaler).
A United States one-dollar note, Washington in the center, ONE DOLLAR along the bottom.

head: dólares — "dollars"
fields: the same German Thaler / Joachimsthaler name, in the Portuguese plural. Regular \-es plural after a consonant-final loan: dólar → dólares (the accent stays on the same syllable, written on the ó).
English dollars; same Thaler family as dólar
The same valley silver, now a sheaf of notes in the hand.
dollars is the same word in the plural.
A hand holding a small fold of twenty-dollar notes, more than one bill in the fingers.
